meta.titre: Ecosystems and Trophic Levels at Ordinary Level: naming each level and following the energy
meta.sous_theme: Ecosystem, producers, consumers and energy transfer

sections.contenu_markdown: A fish pond behind a farmhouse holds tiny floating algae, small animals that eat them, fish that eat the animals, and bacteria at the bottom that rot whatever dies. These living things and the water, light and temperature around them form one ecosystem. GCE papers ask you to name the trophic level of an organism, to explain why plants come first, and to follow how energy is passed on. A clear method makes these questions routine.

items: Green plants make food by photosynthesis, using light energy.
Animals feed on plants or on other animals.
Respiration releases energy from food, and some of that energy escapes as heat.

sections.titre: Ecosystems, trophic levels and the one-way flow of energy
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Habitat | The place where an organism lives |
| Population | All the organisms of one species in a habitat |
| Community | All the populations living together in a habitat |
| Ecosystem | A community together with the non-living (abiotic) factors around it, such as light, temperature, water and soil, acting as one unit |
| Producer | An organism that makes its own food from simple substances, usually by photosynthesis |
| Consumer | An organism that gets its food by eating other organisms |
| Decomposer | A bacterium or a fungus that feeds on dead remains and wastes and returns nutrients to the soil |

### Trophic levels
A **trophic level** is a feeding level in a food chain. Count from the producer.

| Trophic level | Name | Feeds on |
|---|---|---|
| 1st | Producer (green plants, algae) | Makes its own food |
| 2nd | Primary consumer (herbivore) | Producers |
| 3rd | Secondary consumer (carnivore) | Primary consumers |
| 4th | Tertiary consumer (carnivore) | Secondary consumers |

Notice that a primary consumer is at the **second** trophic level. Decomposers feed on the dead remains from every level, so they are not given a number.

### Why green plants are at the first level
Green plants contain chlorophyll and trap light energy to make food by photosynthesis. This changes light energy into chemical energy stored in food. All other organisms depend on this food, directly or indirectly, so plants must come first.

### Energy flow
The Sun is the source of energy. Only a small part is passed from one level to the next, about **10%** is a useful working figure. The rest is lost as heat from respiration, in movement, in undigested faeces and in parts that are not eaten. For this reason food chains are short and the energy flows in **one direction**. Nutrients, unlike energy, are recycled by decomposers.

variantes.nom: Finding the level of an organism
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a chain or a web is given
variantes.contenu_markdown: Find the producer, which eats nothing. Count the steps from the producer: the producer is level 1. In a web an organism can be on several levels, for example an animal that eats both plants and herbivores.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question gives the energy of one level and a percentage transfer
variantes.contenu_markdown: Multiply the energy by the percentage to get the next level. With 10% transfer, move the decimal point one place to the left at each step. To find the percentage transferred, divide the energy of the higher level by the energy of the lower level and multiply by 100.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a first statement and a second statement are given and you must decide how they relate
variantes.contenu_markdown: Decide first whether each statement is true by itself. Only if both are true ask whether the second really explains the first. A true fact that is not the reason is a common trap.

sections.enonce_markdown:
In a fish pond, the feeding relationships are: algae are eaten by water fleas; water fleas are eaten by small fish; small fish are eaten by large fish; bacteria decompose all dead remains. The algae in the pond hold 8000 kJ of energy. Assume that 10% of the energy is passed on at each step.

(a) Name the producer.
(b) Give the trophic level and name of the small fish.
(c) How much energy reaches the large fish?
(d) Why are the bacteria not placed on a numbered level?

etapes.action: Find the organism that makes its own food.
etapes.justification: Algae contain chlorophyll and do not feed on other organisms.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The producer is the algae (trophic level 1).

etapes.action: Count the steps along the chain for the small fish.
etapes.justification: Algae level 1, water fleas level 2, small fish level 3.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The small fish are secondary consumers at the third trophic level.

etapes.action: Apply the 10% rule at every step.
etapes.justification: The large fish are three steps above the algae, so the transfer is applied three times.
etapes.resultat_markdown: 8000 kJ -> 800 kJ (water fleas) -> 80 kJ (small fish) -> 8 kJ (large fish).

etapes.action: Explain the position of the bacteria.
etapes.justification: They feed on the dead remains of organisms from all levels, not on one level only.
etapes.resultat_markdown: They are decomposers and act at every level.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) **Algae**. (b) **Third trophic level, secondary consumer**. (c) **8 kJ**. (d) Decomposers break down dead remains from every level, so they do not belong to one numbered level.

items.erreur_markdown: Plants are at the first level because they are the biggest or the most numerous.
items.pourquoi_faux: Position in a trophic level depends on how the organism gets its food, not on its size or number.
items.correction_markdown: Plants are at the first level because they make food by photosynthesis, which supplies energy to the other organisms.

items.erreur_markdown: All the energy of one level is passed to the next one.
items.pourquoi_faux: A large part is lost as heat, in movement and in uneaten or undigested material.
items.correction_markdown: Only about 10% passes on, so the energy decreases at each level.

items.erreur_markdown: A herbivore is a secondary consumer at the third level.
items.pourquoi_faux: The count starts at the producer, so a herbivore is the first consumer and is at the second level.
items.correction_markdown: A herbivore is a primary consumer at the second trophic level.

items.erreur_markdown: Energy is recycled in an ecosystem like nutrients.
items.pourquoi_faux: Energy is lost as heat and cannot be reused by plants, while nutrients return to the soil through decomposers.
items.correction_markdown: Energy flows in one direction; nutrients are recycled.

items.erreur_markdown: A mushroom growing on a dead log is a producer.
items.pourquoi_faux: A mushroom is a fungus with no chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise. It feeds on dead matter.

items.enonce_markdown:
In a cassava farm, a cassava plant is eaten by a grasshopper, the grasshopper is eaten by a lizard, and the lizard is eaten by a hawk. A fungus grows on dead cassava stems.

Name the trophic level and the type of each of the five organisms.
items.solution_markdown:
- Cassava plant: **producer**, 1st level.
- Grasshopper: **primary consumer**, 2nd level.
- Lizard: **secondary consumer**, 3rd level.
- Hawk: **tertiary consumer**, 4th level.
- Fungus: **decomposer**, not on a numbered level.

items.enonce_markdown:
The producers of a grassland hold 25000 kJ of energy. About 10% of the energy is passed from each level to the next.

(a) Calculate the energy held by the tertiary consumers.
(b) In a different ecosystem the producers hold 40000 kJ and the primary consumers hold 3000 kJ. Calculate the percentage of energy passed on.
(c) Name two ways in which energy is lost between two levels.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Producers 25000 kJ; primary consumers 2500 kJ; secondary consumers 250 kJ; tertiary consumers 25 kJ. The answer is **25 kJ**.
(b) 3000 / 40000 x 100 = **7.5%**.
(c) Any two of: heat from respiration; movement; undigested material lost as faeces; parts of the organism that are not eaten.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Explain why a food chain rarely has more than five trophic levels.
(b) Explain why many more grasshoppers than hawks can live in the same area.
(c) Suppose all the decomposers in a forest were killed. Predict two effects on the ecosystem and explain them.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Energy is lost at each step, so after four or five steps too little energy remains to support another level.
(b) A hawk is at a higher level and receives only a small part of the energy of the lower levels, so the area supports only a few hawks and many more organisms of the lower level.
(c) Dead plants and animals would not be broken down, so **dead matter would pile up**; the **nutrients would not return to the soil**, so plants would grow poorly and, over time, the producers and then all consumers would decline.

items_markdown: An ecosystem is a community together with the non-living factors around it.
Trophic levels are counted from the producer: producer 1, primary consumer 2, secondary consumer 3, tertiary consumer 4.
Green plants are at the first level because they make food by photosynthesis, using light energy.
About 10% of energy passes on at each step, so food chains are short and energy flows in one direction.
Decomposers act on the dead remains of every level and recycle nutrients.
